projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Raymond Firmani was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. Don't just say yes. Say, "During the day I was --"

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Yeah, well, before you start, I was there the last eight months of the war, I -- in -- in '44, Christmastime.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: That was fine. No. I just -- I just --

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Oh, you just gave an example.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Because, see, I don't -- as you know, being in the film, so I -- I -- you won't hear me at all in this whole documentary.

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Oh, I see. All right. I got you.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: You're just going to hear you, so I have to know what you're -- you're actually answering or saying.

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: I understand completely.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. Are you ready?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Ready.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. Uh, now, I want you to state your name and spell your last name.

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: All right. My name is --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And look at me.

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Look at you?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Sorry. My name is Raymond Alexander Firmani. The last name is F, like in Frank, i-r-m-a-n-i. Firmani.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. Now, I'm going to ask you -- and you -- it's -- it's more of you telling the story. It's more of you telling the story, so I'm going to ask you three questions, and you can go from one to the other to the other. That's all about. The first one is where did you grow up, the second one is -- is who your parents were and what they did, and the third one, do you have any brothers and sisters. So you can start by telling me the first one, where did you grow up, and then about your parents and --

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: All right. A little -- little bio?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Okay. I was born in Camden, New Jersey, September the 19th, 1921. My mother and father were immigrants. They immigrated from Italy. And I had four brothers -- five brothers and one sister. That was their family. And we moved from Cam -- my father died when I was very young, 1926 to be exact, so my mother moved down to Wilmington. Her brother was working here at the time. And so -- and -- oh, as far as schooling, I started (?number eleven?) school -- do you remember where that used to be, where St. Anthony's was -- I went-- I went there and I went to lower school and to (Byer) Junior High, and I graduated from Wilmington High School. That's briefly the -- my bio, as far as being here.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: What about brothers and sisters?

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Oh, brothers and sisters? Yes, there are -- well, two brothers, Dominic and Chip, and my mother remarried, and there were -- and she had another three children. There was Albert, Sandra, and Joe. When the war started I was the eldest of the family. My mother and father were separated -- stepfather, so being the eldest I figured I had to go. So I picked aviation because I was interested in aviation. I was building little model airplanes. In those days you could buy a little kit for about ten cents and make it fly, you know, and it was fun, but I think what really, really prompted me, of course, Vietnam -- I mean, not Vietnam, Pearl Harbor, of course, excited all -- all of us. Everybody wanted to go. But the thing that makes it most -- I think the thing that really made me interested in photography was when I saw a motion picture I wanted wings. It was show, the cadet training and the flying, and I don't know where I had the audacity to think I could fly. I didn't even have a driver's license for a car. So -- Do you want me to go on from this?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: No. No, go -- tell me -- tell me, and I want you to repeat, December 7th 1941, what do you remember about that date, so tell me when you found out about Pearl Harbor, what your feelings were, so say "December 7th 1941" and then tell me the story.

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Well, December the 7th, 1941, was a -- on a -- was a Sunday, if I remember correctly, and I remember -- I think that -- what I don't remember is whether I was going to church or coming back from church. I heard this, and it was a shock, everybody -- people gathering around newspapers, and those days they had what they call extra. I think about, oh, a few hours kids were on the streets selling papers, "Extra extra," you know, "read all about it," and -- and, of course, we were shocked, and -- and the -- and the following -- days following that, when we got the results of what happened and the President made his declaration of war, and the whole country was really into it. There was no such thing as holding back. You realized you had to do something. And even -- and remember then -- so '41 I was only 20 years old, and then I was working for DuPont Company by that time. Should I go on from there?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Yeah, so -- so okay. So you worked at DuPont, so you were actually working working then, and you were out of school?

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Yes. I -- I -- I took the academic course, but we -- they couldn't afford to send me to college, so I -- I got a job at -- at Chambers Works at DuPont Company as a -- a safety clerk, but actually it entailed some photography. I took progress photos of the plant when it was being built there. And -- and so what we did -- here's a little interesting story. We decided to -- a couple of friends of ours said "Let's get into the Air Force." So to do this you had to go up to Philadelphia to take a test at the customs house, so we took a train up there, about three hours, and as we entered other guys were coming out, and there was a sign "Army tests, Navy tests." I said, "Which -- where -- where do we even want to go?" He said -- so we decided, well let's try -- I said, "I got an idea," I said, "let's try the Army," because they told me it was a little bit more math, the other was more physics. So I said, "If we flunk that we'll go through the Navy." As it was we were all -- all three of us were accepted by the Navy and as a reserves so that meant we had to wait until they called us. So that's how I got into the Air Force, and I was called in later.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did -- where did you live in Wilmington?

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: At -- at the time of -- at the time of enlistment I lived on Lincoln Street, between Second and Third. And when I returned my family had moved to Clayton Street.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Which block on Clayton? I'm just --

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Oh, between Second and Third.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: On Clayton?

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: On -- oh, on Clayton Street, no. Clayton was between, let's see, wait a minute, Fourth -- Third and Second. It was houses facing the -- the park. It was a beautiful place in those days, big sycamore trees.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: A little different now.

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Oh, yeah, a lot of -- lot of football games and stuff. An exciting time, really.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So you worked at DuPont and you went up and you signed up, and they put you in the reserves right away?

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Yes. You had -- in the reserve they give you a slip that -- so you can show. I -- I was a -- an air raid warden all during that period. I volunteered as an air raid warden, preparing against the possibility of anything happening.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did you work at the tower up at Eighth and Rodney or --

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: No, I -- I -- as -- as an air raid warden I -- I was the -- more or less the custodian of the -- two or three blocks. They give you a hat and a band, and that was -- but -- but when I was in the -- working for DuPont, waiting to be called, I realized it was going to be quite a lot of math and physics, so what I did, I took a couple courses at Calvin -- at the Wilmington High School. They had physics and math. Fortunately I was in perfect health, but I really got a lot of help from the chemists. They were most helpful. They knew -- and I --I got instruction, and so -- so when I went in the service I was really prepared. I did pretty well in -- academically in the tests and so forth.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: What -- do you remember what -- where -- where did you go first in the service? Tell me -- tell me a little bit -- start your story in the service.

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Yes. When -- when they first called us -- being a reserve, I was called up. When they first called I was to report in Miami Beach for boot camp. Can you imagine going to Miami Beach for boot camp? So we took a train there, and when we arrived we marched into -- this was actually Miami Beach, a little island, these beautiful hotels, and we were carrying our suitcases and these guys hanging out the windows, "You'll be sorry," and it was just exactly at the time when Clark Gable was called to officer training there, OTS, and it was loaded with women. All the women were trying to get a glimpse of him. Of course we cadets could hardly leave our hotels, the rooms. There -- when we say hotel rooms, they were stripped, of course, but -- and from there I went to Kent State University, and there they -- that's when we got the physics and math and meteorology and all the other things to help us out. It was all accelerated, wonderful teachers, and that's where we got our first taste of flying, ten hours in a Piper Cub with an instructor. And it was exciting, more or less a promise of things to come. Of course, all along the time there were taking tests or they'd give you tests for adaptability and so forth. And from there we went to Kelly Field in Texas and San Antonio. Hot place but very nice. And there we got more -- we received more training in, oh, more or less Army things, like dot and dash, what am I talking about, Morse code, we had to learn Morse code, we still got more information on -- oh, we had to qualify with a pistol, a .45. I qualified as an expert. I realized that gun -- I only weighed about 128 pounds in those days, and I'm not a big guy. I was five six. And I held that .45 up, it weighed a ton. I said, "I'll never qualify," so I went out to the barracks and I picked up a big stone and I held it out there every day until I developed a pretty good arm, and darned if I didn't qualify as an expert, you know, for short distance and far distance. But from there I went on and -- let's see -- oh, from there then we went into real flying. We went to primary. Primary was in Sikeston, Missouri. And there we flew the PT-19, which was a -- a little bitty model plane, two-seater, made of wood, plywood, a real nice little airplane, and that's where I flew solo. A little interesting affair there. I remember one time we were waiting to check our planes out and I saw one of my buddies coming across the field -- and it was very cold there, it had been snowing, there was some snow on the field -- carrying his parachute. He came back, he was cold and barefooted. No boots, that is. So -- see, when you flew those airplanes you wore a fur suit, fur-lined suit, pants and hat, and the boots over your -- over your heavy socks. So he come back -- what happened -- see, after you solo you can go up and fly by yourself, after you get instruction. Well, he was -- and they'd go up and practice things you want. Well, he was -- he was going to do a loop, so he -- he tries to pull the stick back and loop, and his seatbelt -- I mean, his safety belt released or it wasn't fastened, either one -- he said it released, but he probably didn't have it on. He falls out of the airplane. He comes down and he pulls his chute, and when he does his boots come off. He's coming down, he lands in the snowy field, he didn't know what to do, so he picks up his parachute, and here he is come walking maybe 2 or 3 miles carrying his parachute. So there was always something funny happening. And then from there we went to basic training, the PT-19, they called the Vultee vibrator. Of course they really shook, the airplane's a very flyable plane but very loud. And that was in Winfield, Kansas. What I remember about that, something funny, I was flying -- I had soloed, and I was flying across country, and before you flew across country you plotted your course on a map and so forth and you kept it on your lap, and you -- you had a computer for wind direction, because if the wind's come from here you have to head into it a little bit, so while I'm flying along, my map, it's in the airplane, and the PT -- BT-17, it has rudders, but there's space below it, and my map dropped and fell to the bottom of the plane. Oh, my gosh, I had -- I knew the heading, but I had get to -- so I'm reaching down between my legs trying to grab this, and I couldn't reach it, so I unfastened my safety belt, and I still couldn't get it. I'm looking over, you know, trying to fly. I said, "I got an idea." I fastened my safety -- "I'll invert the plane, and when it comes down I'll catch the map," which I did. Wrong. What happened, Dixie cups, car wrappers, dust, dirt, that plane -- plane probably hadn't been inverted in the last 20 years. Like a smoke screen. So finally I did get the map, I finished my tour, I come back I was really filthy because all the dirt of weeks had been there. But anyhow, from there I went onto advanced training an AT-6. This was in Eagle Pass, Texas. And they never -- it was always something to remember, one outstanding thing. What I remember about this was after I soloed, we were flying the first high altitude mission, at 10,000 feet -- this was a big deal in those days. And what you did, you carried a little cylinder of oxygen, and you put a thing in your mike like a pipe in your mouth and you opened this valve and you took a little oxygen. Well, I was flying on my instructor's left wing, and we were flying under simulated combat conditions, and that's no radio -- radio silence. I meant radio silence. So all of a sudden I look over and I'm flying in beautiful position, you know, and my instructor's going (gesturing). I thought he was waving, and I'm waving back. Finally he says, "Jiminy Crickets, Firmani," he says, "you're on fire. Get the heck back to base." Well, I had been looking out of the cockpit, see, and I looked and my windshield was splattered with oil and the smoke was coming down from this, because I couldn't see it, holy smoke, so I hit the thing, I went down, and I looked and I said, "It looks like I've been shot," trailing all this smoke, and I came -- I opened up about a couple thousand feet, and low and behold it's overcast, I don't know where the heck I am, because it's like when you're a passenger in a car, if you're not aware, the driver's aware. I didn't know where I was. I said, "Holy smoke, what can I do?" So I figured "Well, I know I'm north of the Rio Grande, being in Texas, I'll head south." So I did, I headed south, and low and behold it cleared up a bit, and quite a bit as a matter of fact. I saw the Rio Grande River, and to the right was El Paso. And I saw there -- or was it Del Rio -- Del Rio, I'm sorry. I think it was Del Rio. Just above Eagle Pass, anyhow. Anyhow, I knew there was a base there that had B-26's, was a two engine -- two engine bombers, so I knew where I was, so I followed the Rio Grande down there. It was my -- Oh, and so when I was flying along I didn't know whether to bail out or not. The thing's smoking, you know, my oil pressure's dropping, but I had no fire, and it takes guts to go leave something which is substantial, and I fastened my safety belt and I stayed about 1,000 feet, about 1,500 feet, I figured I had enough space to jump. So I'm smoking along, I said, "I hope I make it." All of a sudden I see the -- the Eagle Pass, so I come in there and I'm -- I'm flying along, and as I come in I report to the Army so-and-so. He says, "Are you having trouble?" I said, "Am I having trouble, I think I'm on fire." That was wrong. I looked down, I see the firebrick, the meat truck, the Jeep, I said, "Man, I must be in worse shape than I thought I was." So I came in and I made my approach like -- just like -- just like I was instructed and made -- even here's an emergency and I'm making it just exactly like I'm told. I cut the throttle, "schick," the thing stops, "Holy smokes," I said, "that stick landed." So I threw the gun to it, pop pop, and she started going, so I had to go around. This time no pattern, I went "shoo," came in, landed, and I -- so I -- I jumped out and ran, and these guys came along and squirted it down. What had happened, it blew a little cylinder -- a little plug out of the cylinders and oil came over, so -- but that's what I remember there. And then from there when I graduated and got my wings evidently they didn't need fighter pilots, they needed bomber pilots more, so after I -- after going home I was sent to Omaha, Nebraska -- Lincoln, Nebraska, as -- as a crew -- picking up a crew, a B-17. I got some transition training there, and we picked up our crew and -- and we left from there, and that's where we went to overseas from there, so that's briefly my training.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Where did you leave -- how did -- how did you get over to Europe?

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: We flew. We -- we -- we -- from Lincoln and flew to Goose Bay, Labrador. It was wintertime, snow, and we landed there and spent a couple of weeks there trying to get weather and flew across the -- across to the Atlantic to England, landed in Wales. And there's where we -- from there we took a -- a train to Eng -- to England to our various bases. I tell you, it's a blue time. You know, it's really funny, oh, I met my wife while I was training in -- in Omaha, and after a very short courtship we married, and -- and my son was born on my first mission, the day of my first mission, December 23rd, overseas. So what -- I went over as a replacement crew. The thing which is interesting, the things about going over there, which reminded me of a little story, when we landed in Wales there was crews which had finished their tours with people -- with crews that were coming in. Well, of course being a air fighter I didn't know what to expect. We started asking these guys, you know, "What's it like?" Oh, boy, they gave us some of the goriest tales, you know. I figured, "Well, I'm dead, that's it." What are you going to do? And I remember that plane ride -- that train ride from Wales -- or through the countryside to -- to my base, it was the -- and also England was very dreary and blue, and I was never so blue in all my life. But I think it's a big mistake to put people going out with people coming in, because as the stories were told they exaggerate a little bit and they see you squirm, they -- and a lot of them may be true, but still -- well, anyhow, that -- that's when the -- they got into -- to our base, we saw the little huts we had to live in and, well --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: At least you had huts.

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Big your pardon?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Some of the guys -- some of the pilots had tents _____ and stuff they were telling us.

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: I'm sorry, I didn't get that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Some of the guys had tents, pilots, some of the other bases.

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: What do you mean ten pilots?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Tents. Tents.

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Oh, tents. Oh, yes. No, in England they have what they call Quonset huts. These were metal huts, structured with a --a front to it, and there was a -- as you -- they had bunks lined up, and -- and there were two crews, officers -- officers and enlisted men were separated. You know, for four officer crews in one decent hut, that's eight people. Funny thing, above the bed you had a shelf, and I never smoked, but I did get the cigarettes. You could exchange them. But you get candy bars. And I had a little box there, and there'd be little field mice that came and eat the darned stuff, so one day I said, "I got an idea," so I took out a couple of them and put them outside the box. Sure enough, they would eat those and wouldn't go into the box. _____, so I was _____ two little bars.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did -- When you arrived there when you were -- when you were assigned your crew you had your crew with you?

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Yes. We -- see, we -- when I -- we arrived there we maintained the same crew. We had a very good crew, good -- very good navigator and bombardier. Our bombardier got a little bit -- on our first mission he got -- he got a little bit flak happy, he couldn't quite hit, so we got a new bombardier, Dawson. His name -- we called him Shack Dawson. He was very good. He could really -- but, see, you must remember, the bombardier sits outs there, he's hanging out there in that Plexiglas, and all that stuff coming up, it takes a lot of guts to sit there and still concentrate and do what you have to do.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did -- So your wife was at home?

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: My wife went back -- my wife was with me all the way until I went overseas, and then she went with her mother, who lived in Omaha, Nebraska.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did -- Let's see, were you scared at all?

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Well, I wouldn't say the word is "scared," because you -- you're busy, you have something to do. I think the worse thing to do is probably be a gunner, because you just sit there and wait, but when you -- when you're flying, you know, you have something to do, your mind is off of it. Now I tell you something funny, you know, those shoe -- we -- we used to wear what they call flak suits. Let me back up just a bit. First of all, you didn't fly every day. There were maybe 50 percent more crews than -- than they -- See, a squadron is made up of about 36 planes 12, 12, and 12, each little box, and these are called squadrons. Three squadrons make a -- a -- a group, and -- I lost my train of thought.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Oh, of the flak.

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Oh. So, well, when we went -- see the thing was, we used to start -- we'd take off from England, finish -- Let me just back up a bit.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: We -- a mission consists of this: You'd get up -- they'd get you up early in the morning, about 5 -- 4 or 5:00, and you'd go to breakfast, and it would be pitch dark, foggy -- many times foggy. As a matter of fact, one time I was on a bicycle. You must remember the -- the lodgings were away from the base, from the field, maybe a mile, and you had to walk it, and most everybody had a bike. When the war ended we gave the bikes to the English kids. I think every English kid in England had a bicycle. We couldn't take them home. But anyhow, I remember this time going down with the bombardier, down this road, fog, and he said, "Ray, I can't see." I said, "I think I see the turn." I made the turn. Wrong. I hit a ditch and went into a big lake -- ditch. I'm hanging upside-down, I could see stars through the fog. But the -- well, the reason I mentioned this, we used to get up very, very early, very dark, we had breakfast, and that's the time we got eggs and stuff. They treated you real good, your last meal, you know. And then you -- you got dressed, and before that then you went in for briefing, and the briefing room is a huge place, they had a big map on there, and you never knew where you were going to go. You see the night before in the officers club if they would be there -- they had a -- we used to have a ball, green on one side, red on the other. Of course green meant nothing, you know, okay, red meant mission. And then they had what they called a flimsy they would post, and it showed formations of airplanes with the names of the crews under it, and you knew whether you had to fly or not, and if you did, then you went back to the barracks and you slept. Anyhow, after they awakened you you had your breakfast, the -- and the briefing consisted of this big room, and they -- and they would tell you where to go, but before that the target was veiled with a big curtain, and they pulled the curtain, and, "Aw, Berlin, oh, my God," you know, you could hear -- you could hear everybody go "Oh," moan, you know, "here we go." And then they would explain, you know, tell you about how you're going to go in and "Here, don't worry about it, there's only 250 guns can bear on you," you know, 250, you figure one of them might get lucky. But anyhow, that was the biggest fear. By the time I was there the fighter opposition wasn't that strong, but the flak was. They had to concentrate a lot on flak. So -- But anyhow, then after that you got your -- you put on -- put your suits on and you go to your minister or your priest, got your holy communion, because I was Catholic, and away you'd go. And we go to -- we were taken to our planes, and we warmed up the planes, and as -- before we'd go, well, you warmed up and then the -- the gunners checked their guns and so forth, they had certain jobs to do. And when you'd take off on signals you'd take off follow -- you would take off and circle above the -- the field in group, and after a group is formed -- it took quite a bit of time -- then you started taking off, raising -- and you started going -- gaining altitude as you went over England, over the _____ Channel, through England, the channel, over France, and then Germany. And just before we got to the target -- now, you -- you wore what they call flak suits, it was a -- like a vest made of steel -- of -- of metal coated with -- coated with a fabric and a helmet, just like a regular GI helmet, to protect you a little bit. But I always sat on a piece of flak. They were shooting, I would say, "Well, hit me in the arm, but please don't hit me," you know, but anyhow, that was -- but as far as fear, there was fear. We used to get flack, and you know if you see the puff of smoke you missed it. You know, it's the ones you don't see that's gonna get you. Of course I saw some planes go down, and we were very fortunate, our group had -- had pretty low losses. I think one reason was that we had a very good group. We flew a very tight formation. I know if I was an enemy pilot I wouldn't attack a real tight formation, because there's plenty of stragglers. If an airplanes a straggler, get behind, they pounce on them, because he's more vulnerable. Our safety was in so many guns. You figure each airplane has about ten guns -- at least ten guns, ten times 36, that's 300 -- you know, that's a lot -- a lot of fire power if it's handled correctly. But if you're -- that would only work if you had good formation and good -- and so forth.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Tell me about your first mission, your anticipation and stuff for your first mission, and then your first mission, where it was.

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: The first mission was in southern -- down southern Germany. I think I said Koblenz. I think I have it on my _____. It was a marshalling yard. You don't know what to expect. Now, we didn't penetrate very deeply there, so consequently there was no really fear factor. I -- I was never really frightened. Oh, I prayed a lot, "Hail Mary, full of grace," you know, going up there and you see that flack going, but the point was it wasn't fear that you'd just go, "Oh, wow," you couldn't do this. You had something -- work to do and you had people depending on you back there, you know. So I -- I know how a duck feels now. But also the noise, of course the roaring of the airplane, the constant roaring. As a matter of fact you must remember we're flying at 25,000 feet. Up there the temperatures sometimes would be at 60 below zero. I remember one time a big clump of ice there -- and -- and -- oh, and you also wore -- in combat you wore a electrically heated suit, because the temperature was below 60 -- it was below zero 60 degrees or so, 40, 60, and consequently when you were sweating, getting hot, through maybe a little fear a little anxiety and a little bit just heat or maybe the suit, you would steam a little bit, and as you breathed it would condense and you would have a big lump here sometimes. And also I remember one time I was sitting there, my gloves were frozen to the -- to the -- to -- to the wheel, because what happened, it'd get hot, you know, and then just holding on so long, and you must remember those missions sometimes took about eight hours, a lot of flying, because both pilots had to do the flying. So that's -- but, like, as far as fear, like I say, if you have something to do and you have people you're responsible for, you just can't think of fear. I wasn't that brave, believe me, but I'm saying was -- it wasn't fear like in trembling, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: As the missions went on, though, did you feel like you were in a lottery, like --

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Well, no, as the missions went on the -- you received figures, for instance, the -- the average flyer was 15 missions or something, and when you got beyond 50 you figure either "Hey I'm just buying it all the way," and you figure I've got sort of a leeway mentally, you think that way. But I remember one time -- see, I -- I was trained as a pilot -- as a fighter pilot, and I -- I -- I always said that seem like every bomber pilot is a frustrated fighter pilot. But I'm glad that it worked out like it did, because a lot of things would've happened to me if it didn't. But I'm trying -- It's -- I -- I diverted there. Let's see. What was the question again please?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: As the missions went on --

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: -- did your -- did you feel your chances --

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Yeah, like in recent -- that's right. You -- you counted each mission. Like I said, after 12 -- 15 or 12 what -- whatever figure it was -- of course, they would say that was the average, and even when you got close -- and you were going for 25, and once you got to 25, of course, they rotated you home. Well, before I got 25 -- I remember -- I remember what I was going to say -- I was -- I said "Well, I -- I'm trying to get back to fighters, B-51's. They had what they call weather scouts. The weather scouts flew before the mission, high altitude, to report back the weather. I had good background in meteorology and so forth, and I figured well, if I get into that and you didn't have to go combat. The idea was get there and get the heck back. So I remember pedaling to one of the fighter bases, I remember this major -- this colonel -- it was a mayor -- a major -- I told him what background I had, and I said I wanted to get back, and he said, "How many missions you have?" And I said -- I think it was 23. He said, "Well you get back when you finish the next two." I figured this guy was giving me _____ confidence, you know. Fortunately it was near the end of the war, so I put my 25 missions in. But like I say, everybody had a goal. The goal was 25 missions.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did any of the -- did -- did -- were -- were most all the crews had that same feeling, you think, I mean, the -- the --

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Oh, sure.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: -- you wanted to leave, wanted to come back? I mean, we had some guys who were these paratroopers who we interviewed that were -- actually head out for the war for three months because of their injury and then right back in and not think anything about it.

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Well, I know there was some crews who volunteered for a second tour. Of course, this -- that meant promotion. Now, see, I became a --a first lieutenant. If I had to go on a second tour I would have been a captain. Some of these guys liked the rank. To me, I had a family at home. I had a wife and a son. My main goal was do my job the best of my ability and get the heck home, survive. That's -- that's what war is all about. Remember, we never even saw the enemy. To me it was just houses and tracks and railroad cars, you know what I'm saying, and I'm sure we did a lot of damage, but that was war and you just did your job. I was only 20 -- born in 1921, and this was '40 -- '44 when I -- 5 when I got out, I was 23 years old -- 24 years old when I got out, in combat at 23, so I was still a very young man.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And your crews must have been even younger than you, some of them?

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: What.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Your crew was probably a lot younger -- some of them were younger than you?

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Yes, oh, we had -- we had Junior, one of the gunners -- we called him Junior -- he was younger -- and, oh, pretty much in about the twenties, most of them twenties, 21, something like that, because -- now, for instance, some of the guys I went with in training at Kent State, these guys had a couple years college, and so you figure they're 18 -- about 20 years old there. And I was a class 44E. I finally figured out what 44E meant was in 1944 it was A, B, C, D, E. It meant in May you're going to gradate, you're going to be ready for combat. That's what it was. It worked out that way.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did your crews play any funny games on you guys or did you play any funny games on the rest of the crews or --

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: I had a tale which --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: I mean you -- you had to have some kind of funny stuff.

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Well, I -- I have one story which will blow your mind, believe me. I tell this several times, and it's unbelievable. See you didn't fly every -- every week -- every day. I get -- I took the three missions at Christmastime, 23rd, 24th, and 26th, during the Battle of the Bulge, but that's unusual, because, remember, we had problems there. But generally you'd fly maybe a couple -- I did 25 missions in about six, seven months, so you can figure out the ratio, about -- about two a week, something like that. But I just come back from -- oh, when you -- whenever you didn't have to fly you'd go to London. A big mistake. I remember one time being in the officers' club, where we slept, the middle of the night, kaboom, a tremendous blast, almost -- I don't remember if I fell out of bed or jumped out of bed and heard ambulances. The next morning I got up and a B-2 had struck about two blocks up and just demolished the block. It's unbelievable. You were safer at the base than you were in London, believe me. A big b-2, that's a big, you know, rocket. Anyhow, so I came back from the base and, gosh, so-and-so -- I forgot who the pilot was -- was shot down. I said, "Oh, darn," you know, he was a -- a pilot of a crew -- of a hut -- next -- hut next to us, and I knew the crew well. So about two days, three days later, I forgot exactly, but I see the tailgunner. We were going to chow, to eat. The tailgunner's walking with a bunch of his buddies and they're discussing something. I said -- went across, "What the heck you doing here? You were shot down." Well, he told us a tale. I think the target was Munich, somewhere on that side. Yeah, it was Munich. It was a low altitude mission near the end of the war, and -- I think at 15,000 feet, which was pretty low for heavy bombers. They made a run, and they made a run, they were followed in by flak -- what they call a flak train. That's a flak train with air guns on it. And they followed it, and so many times the flak just parallels the course. But anyhow, after they dropped the bomb it was hit. The pilot gives instructions "Prepare for ditching." Well, each position has something to do, for instance the waist gunners, he throws the -- pulls the lever and the -- the panels where the guns are open up -- opens up the ship for jumping out safe, and each one -- now, the tailgunner, his job was to go -- he'd disconnect his microphone -- he had -- he wore a float mike and earphones. You have -- to -- to get out you have to disconnect this. To go back you had to go back about eight feet or so and pull the handle, which jettisoned a door for him to jump out of, and he went -- he crawled back and plugged himself in and he's sitting there with a gun and -- and doesn't hear anything, no chatter. Normally there's some chatter on the intercom. He calls back, "Tailgunner to pilot. Tailgunner to pilot, bombardier," no one's answering. He pulls the thing and says "What the --" he goes back, the plane's empty, air coming through there, completely empty. He's all by himself and he's looking out there and the engine is smoking, but it's on automatic pilot and flying beautifully. So oh, my God, what had happened, when he pulled his -- disconnected his communication and pulled the handle the pilot said, "Get the heck out of this thing," and they all bailed out. He didn't get that instruction -- that -- so by the time he goes back they had been gone, so he said, "Here I am sitting on this darn munitions box," he said, "I knew I had to get out of this thing sooner or later, so --" but he didn't have the guts. He chickened out. He said, "I was afraid to bail out." But finally -- but I wanted to _____ -- you got shoes, and you wore them over -- ___________ boots so you always take your regular shoes -- high top -- your Brogans with you and you tied them over here, because if you bailed out, you didn't want to spend the rest of the war in boots. You had to have shoes. So he says, "I'm tying my shoes on here and finally getting nerves to jump." He says well, he goes over, he parachutes and pulls the cord and he lands. All of a sudden he sees a Jeep come picks him up, he had landed in France. What had happened, when the bomb -- when they were hit the pilot hit 270 back west toward France, and he delayed himself long enough he went to -- France is not that big a -- the plane's going 300 miles an hour -- he landed in France. The rest of the crew was taken prisoners of war, he lands, they put him in a Jeep, fly him -- take him back to England, and he gets back in two or three days. The rest of them were all taken prisoners of war. Isn't that --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: What was the hardest part of your service?

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Well, what do you mean -- what do you mean by hardest? The hardest part of service, what do you mean by that, like what?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: The toughest time for you when you were in. It seems like, though, that you had -- you had a pretty good attitude from day one until the day end.

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: I'm always positive about things. I never thought about not coming home. I never did. I always figured I was going to do it. I think you -- you have to take that attitude, because if you take the other -- the least bit of confusion -- for instance, like I told you, many times airplane came back with holes in it and we got hit that time, and, like I told you many guys get shaken up. I figured "Hey, it only takes one little piece to kill you," and -- but the main thing was I think what happens when you're that young, you're the intrepid flyer, you know, "Nothing's going to happen to me," and that was the attitude you had -- you had to be that way. And we were 8th crew, and being the 8th crew you got responsibility. You had to -- because if you missed, everybody missed. If you did poorly, everybody did poorly.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: What do you want the generations to come to know and remember about World War II?

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Well, I want the people to remember World War II was a very bloody affair, because the ones who made it are very darn lucky. It makes you wonder about what -- war doesn't solve anything, you know, I think there should be other ways to do things. I honestly -- I'm here, I'm 83 years old. I honestly think the way to do this is a world court. I'm going to get a little political, because it means giving up a little sovereignty, but if you give up a little sovereignty, and look at the lives we're wasting, look at the money it's cost, the destruction. It's ridiculous. I'm sure generations from now when people solve their problems they'll say "Those people were dumb. They were really dumb." I hope -- I don't like war. No one likes war. Of course people say we had to do it. I'm sure we probably had to do it. But there's got to be a better way. There's got to be a better way.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: What -- what do you think -- as -- as far as reading and stuff goes since the war, what -- what do you think -- have the history folks left anything out, have they --

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Have people left anything out about the war, you mean? Well, the thing that strikes me the most, whenever I -- whenever I used to come out of the PX these little kids would be out there, the smaller children, little children, they would always be -- they wouldn't be begging. That's one thing I got to say about those little English kids, they never begged. They'd just be there. And you'd go over and they -- they wanted candy, you could see they did, and you were glad to do it. And you felt so sorry for them. And all children. I'm sure the German children, the same way, you know, and here were adults. You figured "There's got to be a better way." I mean, what -- so I think maybe what they missed was the -- the compassion about it. Of course I think you'll find -- you'll see movies where you have these pilots -- you know, gung-ho pilots. I didn't see anything like that. People were like these kids out of high school, kids out of college, had a job to do, they wanted to get the job done, come home, and hope for the best -- best world for the children. It's always about children. And I -- I thought about -- many times about the bombings, of course, the destruction. I was fortunate I didn't have to see it, because if I saw it I probably -- probably would have had a nervous breakdown. I -- I -- and also, too, another thing, too, people don't realize how the civilian population suffers. You know, we had -- there was a lot of destruction in Germany. I'm sure the people suffered like mad there, and their leaders are to blame for a lot of the destruction, ______ the people. Now, look at here, I remember the -- in England, in the underground, people -- people sleeping there. They had to sleep there, children. They -- they lived there, the little mothers and families, and they're sleeping on mattresses and so forth, trying to survive. _______ there's got to be a better way. And the people have to go -- realize that war is a very, very, very last thing to go into. It's -- it's not worth it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Why do you think that you guys are called the greatest generation?

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Well, I'll tell you one thing -- Why they call -- they called us the greatest generation, I think, because I'm sure that probably if Hitler had won, the whole world would be a different place, there's no doubt about it in my mind, because he had plans of grandeur, like other leaders have had, you know, you've had your Julius Caesars and you've had your -- all these other guys who wanted world -- world domination. You're never going to make an American different than American. You're never going to make a Frenchman more than -- different than a Frenchman. He's always going to be a Frenchman. But, you know, people realize one thing. Here's one thing I've often said: You are -- your nationality is by accident of birth. I mean, if you're -- if you're -- if you were born in France you would be French. Would you be any different? If your mother and father had been there you would be exactly what you are. So nationalities -- it is going to have to be realized that nationalities are by -- are determined by accident -- by birth of accident. So knowing this, realize that people -- your opposition is just like you, they have the same feelings, the same hurts, the same pains, so I think that people of good will can get together and make this a better world. I think we can.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, when you -- tell me about when you got out and you -- you got -- you had your 25th mission and --

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Oh, okay. That's a little interesting. After -- when the war ended, of course, there was great jubilation in our barracks, we were happy we made it, survived, and then what I remember mostly about that was the -- there were soldiers from -- I think -- this one I remember was a Polish soldier was going to be repatriate -- go back home, he came with a great big thing on his back. He -- he wanted cigarettes. He was exchanging cigarettes for liquor. Of course, cigarettes was like money in those days, had a good exchange, and I remember that. And, of course, I remember -- oh, I flew back the other way too. I flew back into -- and one -- two main, I think -- I forgot where it was now -- just a moment. Anyhow, when we landed, of course, we were questioned again and so forth and you got things to turn in, some of us had papers to fill, out and I had a big bunch of records of the crew that had to be given into -- had to be turned in, and I remember I had a .45 pistol, you know, I wanted to keep it, but I said, "No, here," I returned it. I'm glad I did, because I noticed on the manifest "returned," you know, but you wanted to keep a souvenir, but I'm glad I didn't. I'm not much for guns anyhow. Never had one, never owned a gun. But when I returned I -- I remember I -- what -- here's an interesting thing too. When the war ended in Europe I came home. Remember, the war was still going on in the Pacific, and my wife at that time was living in Texas with her father. He was a instructor -- a tank instructor at the Red River Arsenal. So while I was there the hydrogen bomb -- I mean, the atomic bombs were dropped and the war ended while I was still on leave there, 30 days of R and R. So from there I went to Drew Field, Tampa, Florida, where I was going to go into B-29's to the Pacific, see. So I told my wife, I said -- I -- I was going to bring my wife with me, but I said, "You better not come," because I had so many points. In those days you got out by points. You got points for medal, for touring time, and so forth, so I had plenty of points, so -- but it still took over a month to get out. So -- so when the war ended there -- well, what I do remember, though, before I go -- went to drew Field and I came home, I was off the -- I got off of the bus and my wife was waiting for me, man, I'm telling you, I felt like a king. I was the happiest guy in the world to see my wife. And Drew Field, let's see, I was there for about a month. I mustered out and came home then I -- my wife and son came into Wilmington and I went back to work for DuPont Company, and I was there 46 1/2 years. So when I got in there I got into photography, I became a photographer, in Jackson Laboratory, which was a research lab. I was there, oh, through a lot of -- lot of the developments of DuPont. Teflon, I knew Plunkett, the chemist who did it. I took a lot of pictures of Plunkett and neoprene and all these things that DuPont worked on in the laboratories, and was very productive. So I guess I worked there for 50 -- 46 1/2 years. Good life, good family. I have two sons, Raymond Charles and Richard Allen, and I've been very lucky. I've been a very, very lucky man.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So you had no -- tell me about you have no regrets about the war, I mean, about joining up and --

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: No. Like I say, I often joke when I say if it hadn't been for Hitler I wouldn't have met my wife, and she was the most beautiful thing. I'll show you a picture. She was a wonderful -- very fine woman. She made me a better man, no doubt about it. I came from pretty humble means in those days. Of course, I don't realize -- you know, I never realized that I'm the first generation American. I never thought of it in this vein. I was -- I -- I was American. You know, I could see how people who were born to immigrants -- how they feel, because I never thought of myself as Italian or -- or -- I was -- I was an American. That's one of my first thoughts always. And I'm sure many others of a different ancestry feel the same way.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did you find -- A lot of the funny stories I've seen are the Irish and the Italians and stuff in these crews or in these battalions or whatever kid around with each other, and it's always --

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: In the crew? Well, you see, you must remember I think you'll find the great exaggeration -- I've seen movies like, you know, the Memphis Belle and some of the other things. The biggest malarkey is all this wise-cracking you hear about. It didn't go on. Many times I'd go into the -- the -- I made it a point to go to the enlisted men's quarters and my crew and talking. We used to sit around just like you sit here, and I'd talk about families -- get through the families. I got my crew, all -- all sergeants, every one of them, and you got to know them. I mean, not that I wanted to know them, but I wanted them to know that I -- being an officer, that's one thing about being an officer in the Air Force, you didn't pull rank. Your sergeant was a -- he was -- he was your buddy, I mean, but as far as joking and playing horse winking jokes, that's greatly exaggerated in movies. Believe me, I know it was in our group, because it was too serious. There was death around. You have next -- tomorrow you maybe dead. So you didn't need hijinks. If you saw this guy was a nut, he should be in the psychiatric ward. But I didn't see any of that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: What major message would you leave for the generations to come?

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: What major -- what major message would I leave for generations to come? Well, I hope we learned from lessons of the past. That's all I can say. Read your history, see what happened, try to make it better. There's got to be a better way. There has to be a better way, believe me. There has to be. Because everybody bleeds the same, everybody dies the same, in agony or happily. So let's make it a better world. That's all I wish for -- for -- for the -- for my -- my great grand -- my children -- I have five grandchildren and five great grandchildren, so I've been a very, very fortunate man. That's why I say if I have any -- any qualms about what happened? No, like I say, if it hadn't been for Hitler I wouldn't have met my wife. For me that was the greatest thing that ever happened and coming home alive. So I'm just kidding on this, of course. But war has its -- I wouldn't say good things, but if anything good comes out of it, it's a miracle, so actually when -- I had -- a miracle was bestowed on me, it really was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, you were -- did you end up -- did you end up at the -- at the lab up -- uptown when they had the studio?

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: No, I was at Jackson Laboratory Chambers Works.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Oh, so you never -- you never made it up to --

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Oh, I know the guys. I know Tolleralski (ph), Dutch.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Who used to run the laboratory up there, though?

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Dutch -- Dutch Grodihand (ph).

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Well, what's his name was up there when I --

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Oh, wait a minute, Alex -- Alex -- oh, a big guy. He's a photographer, Alex --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Yes. I can't --

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: -- Henderson. Alex Henderson. Do you remember him?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And there was -- well, there was also a German -- do you remember the German guy that was the printer?

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Dutch -- well, the German guy was Dutch Grodihand.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Yeah, but there was another guy too?

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Another guy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Younger guy. Probably in his early sixties right now.

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Well, that's -- I don't remember --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did a lot of stuff with Curtis. Ended up actually working, I think -- from -- from DuPont he went to -- I think he might have gone down to Tri-Color --

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Oh, he --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: -- across the street from --

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: The other way around. From Tri-Color he went -- no wait, yeah, he went to Tri-Color.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Then he went to DuPont?

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Then he went to DuPont. I know he was a young kid. Very nice handsome boy. I remember him. I don't remember his name. No. I remember him.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: What do you want to do? Do you want to do some -- are any of those -- can you give me those photos out of that book? Are they --

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: They're all the on that disc.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: No. No. No. No. I wanted to put one in front of you.

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Just hold one. Yeah. The one -- ______________+ -- can you just hold it in front of you?

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Yeah. A little glare? Yeah, this was when I got my distinguished flying cross. I was a better looking guy in those days. I wasn't born this way.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: You look great. Look right at me.

sp.speaker: Raymond Firmani
sp.p: Oh, and look back? When this is compiled will it be available or --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Here's what we're going to do. The 20th -- thanks. The 20th of October -- [End of file]
